back: A cheap draft proposes γ tokens; the target checks them all in one forward pass and keeps a prefix of them, plus one token of its own.

front: Minimum and maximum tokens per target pass?
back: At least 1 (the replacement or bonus token) and at most γ + 1 (all drafts accepted plus a bonus).
Accept a draft token if it equals the target's argmax; at the first mismatch emit the target's argmax instead.
Accept draft token x with probability min(1, p(x) / q(x)). On rejection, sample from norm(max(0, p − q)).

front: Why is the output exactly the target's distribution?
back: P(x) = q·min(1, p/q) + (1 − β)·p'(x) = min(p, q) + (p − min(p, q)) = p.
Σ min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 − total variation distance between target and draft.
(1 − α^(γ+1)) / ((1 − α)(γc + 1)), with c = draft step time ÷ target step time. Assumes verify costs one step.

front: Can speculation be slower than plain decoding?
Why does speculation stop helping at large batch?
back: A pass processes B × (γ + 1) tokens; past the ridge point it is compute-bound, so verifying costs more than one step and rejected tokens waste FLOPs.
No. Prefill is already parallel and compute-bound; speculation reduces time per output token.
At long contexts KV-cache reads dominate, decode stays memory-bound even at large batch, so speculation can raise throughput there too.
Extra heads on the target's last hidden state predict tokens several positions ahead; tree attention verifies candidates; typical acceptance is not exact.
A light head drafts next-layer features from the target's features plus sampled tokens; keeps the exact acceptance rule.
Find the last generated tokens in the prompt and propose what followed. Nearly free; best when output copies input.

front: What happens to KV entries of rejected tokens?
back: They are rolled back in both draft and target caches; with paged KV that means freeing slots in the last blocks.
